Gulmohar Aftercare and the Measurement Quarter

Bengaluru, Sunday 11 October 2026. A satisfaction programme that three constituencies read three different ways, ten weeks before the only wave that is contractually binding.

1 The night before

Rain had been falling on Indiranagar since four in the afternoon, and by nine o'clock the power had flickered twice. Aparna Nadkarni, co-founder and Chief Product Officer of Gulmohar Aftercare, had the Dubai quarterly business review deck open on one screen and, on the other, an email from Toronto that she had now read three times.

The deck had been presented five days earlier, on Tuesday 6 October, in a glass-walled room on Sheikh Zayed Road. Slide four carried one number in 96-point type: Programme NPS +37, up from +23 in the June wave. Adil Nanji, Group Customer Experience Director at Ghaf Retail Holdings, had photographed the slide on his phone and said, mildly, that his own board would like it. Anusha Natarajan, who runs customer success out of Singapore and had flown in for the meeting, had allowed herself to look pleased.

The email from Akanksha Nigvekar, Gulmohar's principal data scientist, had arrived at 2:41 a.m. India time on Friday 9 October. Its subject line was "recommend-question base - please read before Monday". Its argument was four paragraphs long and contained no adjectives. The +37 had been computed over the respondents who completed every question in the survey. Computed over everyone who actually answered the recommend question, the same wave returned +27. Computed over everyone who answered the recommend question but excluding the Arabic-language forms served through a survey template in which the response scale may have rendered in the wrong order, it returned +20.5, a shade below the June wave's +21.0 — though June's own Arabic responses cannot be separated out for the same treatment, and half a point is well inside the sampling error of either figure.

Clause 11.4 of the master services agreement would be measured on the wave fielded in the quarter ending 31 December 2026. At or above +45, Gulmohar earned the whole service-quality pool of ₹8.16 crore. Between +30 and +44 it earned half. Below +30 it earned nothing and owed Ghaf a service credit of ₹3.40 crore. Schedule 6 of the same agreement defined the respondent base as "respondents completing the Survey" — the base Akanksha's email argued could not carry the inference the company was drawing from it, and the only base the contract recognised.

At 8:30 on Monday morning there would be fourteen people on a video call. The board met on Thursday 22 October. Ghaf's own board would decide on renewal by 31 January 2027. Aparna wrote four words on the back of a courier envelope, which was the only paper within reach: which number, and whose?

2 Company history, and the decision that still binds

Gulmohar Aftercare was registered in Bengaluru in August 2019 by Aparna Nadkarni, then a product manager who had spent four years building logistics tooling, and Aditya Nukala, who had sold networking hardware to Indian retail chains for a decade and knew exactly how badly appliance service worked. Their first product was unglamorous: a booking and dispatch app for independent appliance repair technicians in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, charging a per-job fee. By the end of FY21 the company was running roughly 9,000 jobs a month and losing money on every one of them.

The turn came in 2021, when a national electronics retail chain asked Gulmohar to run the after-sales service promise attached to its extended protection plans. The retailer did not want an app; it wanted a service-level guarantee, a single invoice, and a number it could show its own management. Gulmohar won the contract, and in winning it made two decisions whose consequences arrived in October 2026.

The first was to build the survey engine in-house, on top of the ticketing database, rather than buy a customer-experience platform. It was the right call on cash at the time: a licensed platform quoted ₹1.9 crore a year against an engineering cost of about ₹35 lakh. But the schema that Amol Nandurkar's team shipped stored one row per survey session — invitation, channel, language, a completion flag, and the final value of each metric — and did not store per-question events. Per-question storage went live only on 1 July 2026, with the redesigned form. Everything the company knows about which question a respondent stopped at, for every wave before July 2026, is an inference from that completion flag.

The second was contractual. When the Ghaf agreement was negotiated in the second half of 2024, Ghaf's procurement team wanted the quality measure defined tightly and Gulmohar's sales team wanted the fee. Gulmohar accepted Ghaf's definition of the respondent base, drafted by people who had never run a survey, in exchange for a fee roughly nine per cent above the figure on the table. Nobody in the room noticed that a completer base rewards exactly the behaviour that an unhappy customer does not exhibit: finishing the form.

Godhuli Capital led a ₹240 crore Series B in March 2023 at a post-money valuation of ₹1,850 crore. The FY27 operating plan the board approved in April 2026 caps salaried headcount at 2,900; the company stood at 2,860 in September, alongside about 11,400 partner technicians working across 38 Indian cities. Aditya has been preparing a Series C at a valuation near ₹3,100 crore, and has told three potential leads that international programme revenue is Gulmohar's second act.

3 The industry

Indian after-sales service for appliances and consumer electronics is a market in which nobody owns the customer and everybody is measured by them. A household buying a refrigerator at Croma or Reliance Digital, or through Flipkart or Amazon, may hold a manufacturer warranty, a retailer protection plan and a platform return window simultaneously, each administered by a different entity. Urban Company has trained consumers to expect a named technician, a slot they chose and a price they saw in advance. Onsitego and the brand-authorised networks compete on turnaround. Gomukh Services, a Mumbai competitor backed by a family office, undercuts Gulmohar on per-job price in the metros and does not publish quality data at all.

Three forces press on the measurement question specifically. The first is distribution: ONDC has made service bookings discoverable outside any single app, which means a growing share of jobs arrive with no app relationship and therefore no in-app survey channel. The second is consent. Since the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's rules came into force, a post-service survey to a customer acquired through a retailer or a call centre requires a consent trail that the retailer's own booking flow does not always capture; Gulmohar's legal counsel has instructed that absent an auditable consent, no survey is sent. The third is money: UPI collection through Razorpay has made per-job payment frictionless, which has pushed the competitive battle away from price and towards the experience of getting a problem handled at all.

Gulmohar's international exposure runs through a single contract. Ghaf Retail Holdings operates 61 electronics and home stores across the UAE and Saudi Arabia and sells a protection plan on roughly one in four large-ticket items. Gulmohar runs the service promise behind that plan in the UAE, employing no technicians there: it dispatches, guarantees and measures, and a Dubai partner network does the work. Ghaf's own differentiation claim to its customers is service quality, which is why Ghaf's procurement team wanted a number in the contract, and why Adil Nanji repeats that number to his own chief executive every quarter.

4 What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In April 2026 the product organisation set itself a target: raise the share of survey respondents who leave a free-text comment, because the roadmap was being argued from scores alone and nobody could say what the scores were about. Annika Neuhaus, Gulmohar's principal designer in Berlin, took the brief. Her redesign, shipped on 1 July 2026, did four things: it opened with two concrete transactional questions (satisfaction with the visit, then ease of getting the problem handled), moved the eleven-point recommend question to position three, added a prompted comment box, and localised the form into Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and Arabic.

On the metric she was asked to move, the redesign worked. Comment rates went from 460 of the 4,180 June respondents (11.0 per cent) to 1,294 of the 4,620 September respondents (28.0 per cent). On the metric nobody was watching, it did something else: because the recommend question now sat behind two others, respondents could abandon before reaching it. In the September Ghaf wave, 4,620 people started the survey and 3,800 of the 4,620 reached and answered the recommend question (82.3 per cent). Of those, 2,900 went on to complete every question.

Through August and September the dashboard that Anusha shows to Ghaf moved from +23 to +37, and three different explanations were offered for it inside the company, each by someone with a reason to prefer it. Avani Nerlekar's service operations team had cut average time-to-first-visit in the UAE programme from 41 hours to 29 hours in the same period, and read the rise as vindication. Annika read it as the redesign surfacing the goodwill that a cold recommend question had been suppressing. Aditya read it as a Series C data point.

Three things have since come into question, and the company does not agree on how much any of them matters. First, the base: the +37 is computed over completers, who are, Akanksha argues, systematically the patient. The 900 respondents who answered the recommend question and then abandoned returned a score of −5.2 — see Exhibit 2, Panel B. Second, the comparison: the June wave put the recommend question first, so in June the completer base and the answered-recommend base describe nearly the same people, while in September they describe measurably different ones. Third, and discovered last, the Arabic form. A reviewer's comment on Annika's July pull request asked whether the 0–10 scale would render left-to-right in an RTL layout; the thread was closed as "ship, verify in v1.1". Verification happened on 12 August, when a Dubai technician's own test submission came back inverted, and the in-app form was patched the same day. The Arabic version of the SMS and email link template — a separate file, owned by the growth team — was not patched until 24 September, six days after the September wave closed. Exhibit 2, Panel C shows what the 540 Arabic responses served through that template look like beside everything else, and the case writer notes only that the company cannot now determine how many of those 540 respondents saw which arrangement, because the rendered scale order was never logged.

Separately, and uncomfortably, the India business has been reporting its own good news. Exhibit 3 shows a September CSAT of 78.0 per cent top-two-box, on a mean rating of 4.16 on the five-point scale — a top-two figure that Avani's team has kept at or just above the 78.0 mark for three consecutive months. Exhibit 3, Panel B puts the effort question to a randomised subsample of 12,000 of those respondents, and on that subsample the two readings part company: 9,384 of the 12,000 (78.2 per cent) rated the visit four or five, while only 6,240 of the same 12,000 (52.0 per cent) agreed that Gulmohar had made it easy to get their problem handled. And Exhibit 4 contains one group that sits against the grain of the other five: across the metros satisfaction and first-visit resolution move together, Bengaluru best on both at 80.0 and 81.0 per cent, but the 33 cities of the Rest of India group return the highest satisfaction of all, 84.3 per cent, on the worst first-visit resolution, 61.0 per cent, and the thinnest survey coverage.

5 The people

Aparna Nadkarni — co-founder, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru
Owns the measurement programme and, by the board's charter, the integrity of what the company reports. Position: the December wave must be measured on a base she can defend in a deposition. Incentive: her reputation inside the company rests on having built the survey programme in the first place. Not saying: she approved the July form change herself, in a fifteen-minute review, without asking what it would do to the base.
Aditya Nukala — co-founder, Chief Executive, Mumbai
Position: the contract defines the base; honouring the definition is not dishonesty, and relitigating it ten weeks before measurement is self-harm. Incentive: a Series C term sheet he hopes to have by March 2027. Not saying: he has already shown the +37 to two prospective lead investors in a deck marked "do not distribute".
Avani Nerlekar — Senior Vice-President, Service Operations, Pune
Runs dispatch, the partner technician network and the India field organisation. Position: the scores are a distraction from parts availability, which is the real constraint. Incentive: her FY27 bonus pays on India CSAT top-two-box at or above 78.0 per cent, which is exactly where September landed. Not saying: her team controls when a job is marked resolved, and a job is only surveyed once it is.
Akanksha Nigvekar — Principal Data Scientist, Toronto
Found the base problem while building a churn model that needed a clean loyalty signal. Position: all three numbers are defensible; the company must say which question each one answers and stop printing one of them alone. Incentive: none that is measured; her objectives are model-quality, not scores. Not saying: she raised the completer-base question in a comment on a dashboard ticket in February 2026 and let it drop when nobody replied.
Amol Nandurkar — Director of Engineering, platform, Bengaluru
Position: per-question storage, a logged scale order and dual-field instrumentation can be shipped by 14 November, in time for the December wave, if the team stops the Tier-2 depot integration. Incentive: an engineering roadmap he has already committed to Avani. Not saying: the 2021 schema was his design, and he knows that history cannot be rebuilt no matter what is shipped now.
Annika Neuhaus — Principal Designer, Berlin
Position: moving the recommend question was correct for the customer and for the quality of what the company learns; the measurement problem is a reporting problem, not a design one. Incentive: comment rate is her stated objective and it rose by seventeen percentage points. Not saying: she saw the RTL comment on her pull request and judged the risk small because UAE respondents "mostly use English anyway" — a belief Exhibit 2 does not support.
Anusha Natarajan — Head of Customer Success, Singapore
Owns the Ghaf relationship and the renewal. Position: whatever is true, Ghaf must not hear it first from Gulmohar's lawyers; and it must not hear it in January. Incentive: her variable pay is weighted on renewal and on the quality pool. Not saying: Adil Nanji called her privately on Thursday to ask whether the jump was "real or a form change", and she said she would check.
Arzan Nagarwala — Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai
Position: the question is an accounting one — whether to provide for the credit now, in H2 FY27, or to treat the outcome as contingent. Incentive: clean audit, predictable cash, no restatement in a Series C diligence window. Not saying: he thinks the sales concession on Schedule 6 in 2024 was the original error and has never said so to Aditya.

6 Exhibits

7 Voices

"I want to be careful about the word 'wrong'. Schedule 6 says completers. We reported completers. If we now report something else, the first question Adil asks is what else we have been computing our own way."

Aditya Nukala, voice note to Aparna Nadkarni, Saturday 10 October, 7:12 a.m. IST

"Three numbers for one quarter is not a scandal, it is what happens when you ask three different questions. +37 answers 'how do the patient feel'. +27 answers 'how do those who told us feel'. +20.5 answers 'how do they feel if we throw away the data we cannot trust'. Pick the question first. The arithmetic is not the hard part — the hard part is that we have no idea what the 20,350 invited customers who never answered that question think, and they are 84.3 per cent of the list."

Akanksha Nigvekar, email to the leadership group, Friday 9 October, 2:41 a.m. IST

"May I say the obvious thing. Our top-two is 78 and our effort score is 52. Those are the same people, same visit, same form. If the customer is satisfied and still says we made it hard, then satisfaction is measuring whether the fridge got fixed and effort is measuring what we put them through. We have been reporting the first and selling the second."

Annika Neuhaus, in the weekly product review, Wednesday 7 October, 14:00 CEST

"Tier-2 is my best CSAT and my worst first-visit number and both are true. Of course they are. I only get to survey the ones where consent came through at booking, and the places where consent is weakest are the places where the customer is most grateful anyone came at all. If you want a number that is not flattering me, measure every job, not every survey."

Avani Nerlekar, service review, Pune, Thursday 8 October

"Hypothetically: if the December wave comes in at +26 and we have said nothing, and then an auditor finds the base note in a ticket from February, what is my disclosure position? I would rather provide ₹3.40 crore in H2 and be wrong than explain a contingency I knew about in October."

Arzan Nagarwala, to Aparna Nadkarni, chat thread, Friday 9 October, 11:40 p.m. IST

"My two proposals in North America both carry the clause as drafted for Ghaf, because it is the clause that wins. If we change our own definition now, I need to know what I am selling on Monday. Both chains have asked who audits the score."

Alvaro Negrete, VP Sales, from Newark, Friday 9 October, 10:05 a.m. EDT

"Anusha, be straight with me — real or a form change? My CEO is quoting +37 in the January board paper. If it is a form change I would rather know now than be corrected by your auditors in February."

Adil Nanji, Ghaf Retail Holdings, WhatsApp to Anusha Natarajan, Thursday 8 October, 4:26 p.m. GST

8 The options, as Aparna sees them tonight

By Sunday midnight she had written four paths, numbered in the order they had occurred to her, which is not the order of their merit. The lettered items A to D in Exhibit 6, Panel B are not paths but instruments: more than one path can buy more than one of them, and the second path can buy none.

Path 1 — hold the line. Report the Schedule 6 base, because it is the contract. Fix the form for the December wave but do not restate September. Tell Ghaf nothing it has not asked. This is Aditya's position and it is not absurd: the definition was negotiated, priced into the fee, and the party it protects is the one entitled to complain about it. The cost is that Adil Nanji has already asked the question, and the answer Anusha gives him on Monday is either candid or it is not.

Path 2 — restate now, before the board. Publish all three figures for September with the bases attached, take the reputational hit while it is small, and propose a joint redefinition of Schedule 6 for the measurement quarter. This is Akanksha's and Arzan's instinct. It puts a ₹7.48 crore swing on the table ten weeks before it is due and in the window when Ghaf is deciding on renewal, and it tells two North American prospects that Gulmohar's numbers move when Gulmohar looks at them.

Path 3 — instrument first, decide later. Ship investment A from Exhibit 6, Panel B by 14 November, run the December wave dual-field — recommend question first for half the sample and third for the other half — and let the data settle the argument. This is Amol's offer. It buys a defensible number from December onward and it buys nothing at all for September. It also requires stopping the depot work, which is the work Avani believes is the only thing that would change what customers actually experience.

Path 4 — change what is measured. Propose to Ghaf that the clause be moved off the recommend question and onto something closer to the thing the two companies are arguing about: effort, first-visit resolution, or the share of jobs closed without a second visit. This is the option Aparna believes in most and trusts least, because it is the option that most obviously serves her own interest — the effort number is lower than the satisfaction number, and the resolution number is produced by Avani's own system.

Each of the four assumes the decision is which number to report. Akanksha's email, read for the fourth time, says something adjacent and more awkward: that Gulmohar has no relationship with the person answering the Ghaf survey at all. That customer bought a refrigerator from Ghaf and a protection plan from Ghaf, and when a technician arrives it is a Dubai partner firm's van in the driveway. Whether that person would recommend anything, and to whom, is a question the survey has never actually asked. Exhibit 2 counts 3,800 answers to a question whose subject may be nobody in the contract.

9 The deadline and the hard constraints

The December wave must be fielded between 7 and 18 December to fall inside the measurement quarter, which means the form, the base definition and any instrumentation must be frozen by 30 November. Amol's four-week estimate for investment A assumes a start on 17 October and a ship on 14 November, which leaves sixteen days of float before the freeze; it also assumes that the platform team's Diwali code freeze, which falls in the week of 8 November and which the team has observed every year since 2022, costs no more than two working days. If it costs a week, the float is nine days.

Money is the envelope in Exhibit 6, Panel B: ₹5.00 crore of one-time spend and ₹4.20 crore of H2 running cost, approved in April. Investments A and C together cost ₹5.50 crore and fit on both lines. Investment B fails on its own, before anything is set beside it: ₹7.40 crore of one-time spend against a ₹5.00 crore envelope, and 42 depot staff against the 40 heads left under the cap of 2,900, at which the company stands at 2,860. Its ₹3.80 crore of running cost would fit, narrowly, if nothing else ran alongside it, but the one-time line and the headcount line do not, so B cannot be funded at all without going back to the board for money and for heads. Contractually, Schedule 6 can be amended only by written agreement of both parties, and Ghaf's procurement director is on leave until 19 October. The DPDP consent position, which legal will not reopen, means roughly a quarter of India's closed jobs can never be surveyed at all. And the board meets on 22 October, where Godhuli Capital's partner sits as an observer and has asked, twice, for a single company-wide quality metric to put in the Series C data room.

10 Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, Panels A and B only, state precisely what population each of the three September figures (+37.0, +27.0, +20.5) describes, and which of them — if any — is comparable with the June figure of +23.0 that was presented alongside it.
  2. On the 12,000-respondent subsample in Exhibit 3, Panel B, the same people on the same form return a top-two-box satisfaction of 78.2 per cent and an effort top-two-box of 52.0 per cent. What, concretely, would have to be true of Gulmohar's service for both to be accurate, and which of the two should appear on a dashboard that a general manager sees weekly?
  3. Exhibit 4 shows the Rest of India group with the highest satisfaction and the lowest first-visit resolution. Set out at least three mechanisms that could produce that pattern, and say what evidence would distinguish them. What does the exhibit's coverage column do to your reading of the national 78.0 per cent?
  4. Exhibit 5 reports a kappa of 0.67 between the human coder and the classifier whose output drives the roadmap review. What decisions currently made at Gulmohar are unsafe at that level of agreement, and what would you accept instead?
  5. Clause 11.4 pays on a definition that Panel B suggests is the least informative of the three. Was the 2024 concession on Schedule 6 a mistake, a fair price for a nine per cent higher fee, or something whose correctness cannot be judged from what the case gives you? What would you now propose to Ghaf, and what would you expect Ghaf to propose back?
  6. It is 8:30 on Monday 12 October and fourteen people are waiting. What does Aparna Nadkarni say in the first three minutes, what does she commit the company to before 30 November, and what exactly does she put in front of the board on 22 October — given that Godhuli Capital wants one number, Ghaf's chief executive is already quoting one, and she now believes that no single number on this page measures what the contract is about?

11 After midnight

At twenty past one she turned the courier envelope over and wrote, under which number, and whose?, a second line: what would I measure if nobody were paid on it? The rain had stopped. On the other screen, Akanksha's email was still open, and below it the unread one from Anusha in Singapore, where it was already a quarter to four in the morning, subject line "Adil — I need words for Monday". Aparna closed the laptop without answering it, and then, some minutes later, opened it again.

Case prepared for classroom discussion in the ISB Software Product Management course. Gulmohar Aftercare, Ghaf Retail Holdings, Godhuli Capital, Gomukh Services and all individuals named in this case are fictitious; companies, regulators and institutions named as market context are real and are described only as market context. Figures are illustrative and were constructed for teaching purposes.

NPS, CSAT and CES: what a satisfaction score can and cannot tell you

Discovery & Design › Quantitative & Market Research — near-expert treatment

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 6 October 2026 in Pune, Pratyusha Vaijapurkar read the slide her chief executive meant to show the board on the fourteenth. Pitara Commerce Network, the quick-commerce grocery business where she was chief product officer, had served 1.86 crore orders in the September quarter. The slide carried one line: relationship Net Promoter Score, 22 in the June quarter, 17 in the September. Beneath it sat a "customer delight programme" costing ₹3.4 crore. Vidyadhar Phansikar, who ran analytics, had sent a note at six that morning: the score fell but nothing got worse. Padraig Ruane, a data scientist working with Pitara from Dublin, attached a confidence interval narrower than the pencil mark on the slide.

Three days later Parthiv Vashishth faced the mirror image in Hyderabad. He was vice-president of product at Rachna Warehouse Systems, which sold warehouse-management software with rugged handheld scanners to 214 enterprise accounts on ₹78.20 crore of recurring revenue. Rachna's relationship NPS had come in at 12.0, up from 9 a year earlier, and the commercial team was pleased. Ravindu Pattanshetti, who ran field service, weighted each account's score by what that account paid, and the number collapsed to 3.7 — because the eighteen largest accounts, carrying ₹34.20 crore of the ₹78.20 crore, or 43.7 per cent of the book, scored lowest of all. Four were up for renewal in January; Vasundhara Pujare, in customer success, still read 12.0 as vindication.

Neither decision turns on "what is our score?" Both turn on what the number measures, over which population, and what must be true for it to mean what the room thinks.

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

A satisfaction metric is a single survey question, asked of a sample, aggregated into one figure. The Net Promoter Score asks how likely a customer is to recommend the firm, on a 0-to-10 scale: 9 and 10 are promoters, 7 and 8 passives, 0 to 6 detractors, and the score is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors — a plain number from −100 to +100, never a percentage. Passives leave the subtraction but stay in the denominator. Fred Reichheld published it in the Harvard Business Review in December 2003; the problem it solved was organisational, since long questionnaires produced reports nobody owned.

Customer Satisfaction is older and more literal — how satisfied were you with this experience, usually on five points, reported as the top-two-box share — with a lineage running through 1980s service-quality work and Claes Fornell's American Customer Satisfaction Index, built at Michigan from 1994. Customer Effort Score, proposed by Matthew Dixon, Karen Freeman and Nick Toman in 2010, asks whether the company made the issue easy to handle, on the argument that ease predicts loyalty better than delight. NPS measures a relationship, CSAT an event, CES friction inside one.

Four camps disagree about what follows. The single-number school, Bain's position, signs that a firm-wide score everyone reads identically, published with verbatims and closed-loop follow-up, changes behaviour more than a superior metric nobody owns; it will not sign that NPS predicts growth better than alternatives in a named industry. The measurement school — Keiningham, Cooil, Andreassen and Aksoy, whose 2007 Journal of Marketing paper failed to reproduce Reichheld's growth advantage — signs that three bands destroy information and the 9-versus-8 cut is convention without warrant, but not that the instrument is worthless.

The behavioural school signs only that stated intent is a proxy to be validated against repeat purchase and renewal, not that attitude is irrelevant, since behaviour arrives too late to steer by. The operational school signs that transaction-level CSAT and CES on a named process are the only measures a team can act on this week.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Everything begins with the frame, not the formula. Pitara invited one survey per household per month after a delivered order, producing 8,40,000 invitations, of which 1,47,000 of the 8,40,000 invitations were answered, a response rate of 17.5 per cent. Every figure below rests on those 1,47,000; the 6,93,000 unanswered are this page's largest source of uncertainty.

Exhibit 1. Quarter ended 30 September 2026. Promoters (9–10) 36,750 + 23,520 = 60,270, or 41.0 per cent; passives (7–8) 29,400 + 22,050 = 51,450, or 35.0 per cent; detractors 11,760 + 7,350 + 5,145 + 3,675 + 2,205 + 2,205 + 2,940 = 35,280, or 24.0 per cent; bands sum to 1,47,000. NPS = 41.0 − 24.0 = 17.0.

CSAT ran on the same responses, from a second question about the order. Of 1,47,000 answers, 55,860 said "very satisfied" and 44,100 "satisfied", so top-two-box CSAT was 99,960 of 1,47,000, or 68.0 per cent; the rest split 23,520 neutral, 12,495 dissatisfied and 11,025 very dissatisfied. A CSAT is a ratio; an NPS is a difference. The mean rating, from first principles, is (5 × 55,860) + (4 × 44,100) + (3 × 23,520) + (2 × 12,495) + (1 × 11,025) = 5,62,275 rating-points over 1,47,000 responses, or 3.825 — and the two move independently, since shifting neutrals into dissatisfied changes the mean and leaves CSAT untouched.

Then precision. Score each response +1 for a promoter, −1 for a detractor, 0 for a passive; the mean of that variable is the NPS as a proportion, 0.17, and its variance is the promoter probability plus the detractor probability less the squared mean: 0.41 + 0.24 − 0.17² = 0.6211. The standard error is the square root of 0.6211 / 1,47,000 = 0.002056, or 0.21 points, so the 95 per cent interval is 1.96 times that: ±0.40 points. For one dark store with 600 responses it widens to ±6.3, which is why store league tables rank noise.

The step usually left implicit is segmentation: Pitara's respondents split into the dense metro core of Pune and Mumbai and the newer tier-2 expansion into Nashik, Kolhapur and Aurangabad.

Exhibit 2. Segment NPS from first principles. Metro: 39,690/88,200 = 45.0 per cent promoters, 15,876/88,200 = 18.0 per cent detractors, so 27.0. Tier-2: 20,580/58,800 = 35.0 per cent, 19,404/58,800 = 33.0 per cent, so 2.0. Weighted by responses, not segments: (88,200 × 27.0 + 58,800 × 2.0)/1,47,000 = 17.0, the pooled 41.0 − 24.0.

In June the metro core supplied 80 per cent of responses and tier-2 only 20. Holding both segment scores where they now stand gives 0.80 × 27.0 + 0.20 × 2.0 = 22.0, precisely the reported June figure, so the whole five-point fall is the shift in mix from 80:20 to 60:40. Nothing got worse. Worse for the slide: tier-2 was budgeted at 55 per cent of responses by March, which at unchanged segment scores yields 0.45 × 27.0 + 0.55 × 2.0 = 13.25.

Rachna's population is small and unequal. The survey went to 1,150 named users and drew 391 responses, a 34.0 per cent response rate, covering 159 of 214 accounts, or 74.3 per cent. Promoters numbered 149 (38.1 per cent), passives 140 (35.8 per cent) and detractors 102 (26.1 per cent), giving 12.0 — but two roles inside each account use different products.

A CES question on the cycle-count reconciliation flow drew 820 responses: 440 of 820 agreed, or 53.7 per cent, and the mean was 3,657 effort-points over 820, or 4.46 on seven points. Both forms circulate, and a team that never says which it reports will one day compare them and conclude effort halved.

4. When the idea applies, as testable claims

One: the respondent population is stable, or its composition is held constant. Pitara fails outright — composition moved twenty points in a quarter and drove the whole headline change. Rachna passes on accounts but fails on roles, because an in-app prompt for supervisors pulled the number down for reasons unrelated to its product.

Two: word of mouth is a material acquisition channel. Pitara passes; referral codes drove a measurable share of new users. Rachna fails, because warehouse systems are bought through tenders and vendor-arranged reference calls, so renewal and seat expansion are its real outcomes.

Three: the movement under discussion exceeds the interval. Pitara passes in aggregate at ±0.40 points and fails at store level at ±6.3. Rachna fails in aggregate: 391 responses on these shares carry ±7.9 points, so its rise from 9 to 12.0 is indistinguishable from nothing.

Four: nobody's pay depends on the number, or it measures the incentive. The idea is actively misleading when a firm enters a harder market, so the score falls as the strategy succeeds; when it fires its worst-served customers, so the score rises with nobody better off; and when the question is asked by the person being evaluated.

5. Hard edge cases

Pushkal Pharma Services, a pharmacy and diagnostics chain under Indian drug-licence inspection and state grievance-redress rules, measured the same visits twice. A tablet handed across the counter by the pharmacist returned 10,488 of 11,400 responses in the top two boxes, or 92.0 per cent. An SMS next day reached 11,500 numbers, drew 2,415 responses — a 21.0 per cent rate — and returned 1,449 of 2,415 in the top two boxes, or 60.0 per cent. Thirty-two points, same customers, a different observer. Where a regulator mandates grievance logging, customers learn the register is for anger.

Hardware-plus-software is Rachna's seam: "the scanner dies by the second shift" is a procurement decision that lands in the product team's NPS. Mature firms ask driver questions separately — device, software, implementation, support, each on its own CSAT — and keep the recommend question for the relationship. What they say they do is close the loop on every detractor; what they do is route device complaints to a queue nobody reports.

Multi-product firms face a problem the formula hides: a Pitara household that loves grocery and was burnt once on the new electronics line gives a 6, and the survey cannot say which product owns that detractor, only that the relationship is damaged. At the organisational seam the score belongs to marketing, the drivers to operations and the follow-up to support, so no team answers for it — and a metric nobody answers for becomes decoration.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The subtraction is lossy, and the loss is where the information is

A score of 17.0 can arise from 41 per cent promoters against 24 per cent detractors, or from 24 per cent against 7: a polarised business with a winnable middle, or a bland one with no enthusiasts. The tell is a team quoting the score without the shares.

Passives are commercially interesting and the arithmetic ignores them

Pitara's 51,450 passives are 35.0 per cent of respondents and contribute exactly zero, yet they are the households a rival converts with one coupon. The tell is a quarter in which the score held while passives grew and promoters shrank, invisible if detractors fell to match.

Mix shift masquerades as quality change, in both directions

The tell is a score movement larger than any driver metric can explain, in a quarter when the business changed shape; the diagnostic is to recompute the prior period at current segment weights. Reading a blend as experience assumes a constant respondent mix, which a growing company never has.

Response weighting and value weighting answer different questions

Rachna's 12.0 and 3.7 are both correct: the first says how users feel, the second how revenue feels. The tell is one unweighted NPS across accounts of wildly different size. Neither is the real number; an expert reports both and says which decision each serves.

Non-response is systematically non-random, and the bias has a direction

At a 17.5 per cent response rate the silent majority is not a random draw: strong views answer, indifference does not. The tell is a score stable to three decimals while churn moves. Sample size shrinks variance and does nothing whatever to bias.

The 0-to-6 band bundles indifference with fury

A customer scoring 6 and one scoring 0 are counted identically. Pitara's band held 11,760 sixes and 2,940 zeros; they want different things, and only one is writing about you in public. The tell is a detractor band whose distribution sank while its share held.

CES locates cost but is silent about value, and no score says what to fix

Rachna's reconciliation CES of 53.7 per cent agreeing points precisely at an expensive process, and cannot say whether customers would pay more; a roadmap of pure friction removal ships steadily while differentiation erodes. Cause arrives only through follow-up questions, coded verbatims or operational data, and the tell is a meeting about a fallen score at which nobody has read a comment.

Each of these numbers is a survey question, with survey design's baggage

Wording, scale labels, scale direction, placement in the flow and whether an incentive is attached move the result by more than most product changes do. The tell is a score that jumps at a quarter boundary when the vendor changed.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the volumes make the arithmetic precise and the interpretation fragile: relationships are thin, switching is cheap, mix shift dominates. What works is continuous transactional CSAT and CES on named flows, with relationship NPS in quarterly waves read against stable segments. In B2B the volumes make the arithmetic fragile and the interpretation rich: with 214 accounts every response has a name, so responses are read account by account and weighted by contract value. The buyer-versus-user split Rachna found is the structural feature of enterprise measurement; averaging across it destroys the signal.

Platforms need one score per side, because the sides' interests are partly opposed. Hardware faces a lag software does not: a scanner is experienced over months, so a post-purchase survey captures the unboxing. AI products break the frame differently, because the same prompt yields a good answer today and a poor one tomorrow, so satisfaction becomes a property of a distribution. By stage, below roughly a thousand responses no quarterly movement is interpretable, while at scale the danger shifts to Goodhart's law. What does not change by stage, geography or sector is the formula — and no credible cross-firm benchmark exists, because response rates and frames differ more between firms than their customers do.

8. Three worked examples

Vipula Freight Exchange: the blend that hid a collapse

Vipula, a truck-load marketplace, cut freight rates in July 2026 to win shipper volume, then surveyed both sides.

The blended −4.8 was reported as roughly flat. Over the next quarter 9,120 of 11,400 active operators remained, a retention rate of 80.0 per cent, against 3,906 of 4,200 shippers, or 93.0 per cent. Capacity left, match rates fell, and the shipper score followed. The pooled weights are each side's response counts: an artefact of fielding, with no economic meaning.

Rasana Beverage Works: where the approach failed, and the recovery

Rasana, a bottled-beverage manufacturer, printed a QR code on the label and offered a ₹20 recharge for completing the survey. Of 62,000 scans, 18,600 started (30.0 per cent) and 14,880 finished: 80.0 per cent of starts, 24.0 per cent of scans. The result was an NPS of 55.0: 9,672 promoters (65.0 per cent), 3,720 passives (25.0 per cent), 1,488 detractors (10.0 per cent), briefed as best in category.

Two tells gave it away. Within the promoter band, 8,184 respondents gave a 10 against 1,488 who gave a 9, a ratio of 5.5 to 1; genuine promoter populations do not cliff like that, but incentivised ones do, because the fastest route to the recharge is the end of the scale. An unincentivised holdout of 2,000 responses through the same code then returned 640 promoters, 760 passives and 600 detractors — an NPS of 2.0, with 352 tens against 288 nines, a ratio of 1.2 to 1.

Rasana dropped the incentive, moved the question to a household panel, and insisted on behavioural validation. Matching 5,400 respondents to retail scanner data, 1,053 of the 3,510 promoters repurchased within ninety days (30.0 per cent), against 378 of the 1,350 passives (28.0 per cent) and 135 of the 540 detractors (25.0 per cent) — 1,566 repurchases, or 29.0 per cent. Fifty-three points of the original score were the incentive, and a five-point behavioural spread cannot support a claim of near-universal advocacy.

Vivechan AI Labs: satisfaction on a non-deterministic product

Vivechan sold a document-extraction assistant to accounting firms. In September 2026 it logged 1,20,000 sessions and collected thumbs ratings on 7,200, a 6.0 per cent feedback rate: 5,328 up (74.0 per cent), 1,872 down (26.0 per cent), reported as a CSAT of 74 per cent.

An audit of 600 randomly sampled sessions found extraction errors in 72, a 12.0 per cent error rate. Among those 72 erroneous sessions only 23 carried a thumbs-down, or 31.9 per cent; the other 49 errors passed silently into clients' ledgers. A review of 300 sampled thumbs-down sessions found 108 of them, or 36.0 per cent, to be correct outputs the user disliked, implying some 674 of the 1,872 negative ratings were not defects. Satisfaction and defect rate were nearly independent, so Vivechan kept the rating as a routing signal and governed quality by an audited accuracy rate.

9. Failure modes, with early warnings and the cost of catching them late

Coaching the score. The warning is a cliff at the top of the scale: many 10s, few 9s, as at Rasana. The diagnostic is "who asks the question, and sees the answer?" Caught late, the series becomes uninterpretable.

Reading mix as quality. The warning is a score movement no driver metric explains; the diagnostic is "recompute last quarter at this quarter's weights." Caught late, the cost is Pitara's ₹3.4 crore on a problem that did not exist.

Averaging across unequal accounts. The warning is an enterprise score improving while renewals get harder; the diagnostic is "what is this weighted by revenue?" Caught late, the cost is a lost renewal: at Rachna, four January renewals sat inside the ₹34.20 crore band scoring −8.3.

Confusing instruments. The warning is a slide calling the reconciliation CES 4.46 in one place and 53.7 per cent in another; the diagnostic is "write the formula next to the number."

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The single number is worth its statistical inefficiency. Steelmanned, the claim is not that NPS measures better but that it mobilises better: a metric a warehouse supervisor, a rider and a chief executive all read the same way produces closed-loop follow-up, and follow-up changes outcomes. The evidence is organisational, not econometric; for this to be wrong, a better-specified metric would have to mobilise as well.

The banding is indefensible. Steelmanned, this rests on the replication record: Keiningham and colleagues found no superiority for net-promoter over mean satisfaction in predicting revenue growth, and the three-band collapse is information-destroying, as Figure 1 shows. For this to be wrong, behaviour would have to be discontinuous at the 8-to-9 and 6-to-7 boundaries — a claim every firm can test on its own data and almost none do.

Stated intent should give way to behaviour. Steelmanned: Rasana's five-point behavioural spread against a fifty-three-point attitudinal gap is the general case, not an anomaly. For this to be wrong, attitude would have to lead behaviour by enough time to be actionable — and here the camp is vulnerable, because for subscription products the renewal signal arrives only at renewal. Unsettled behind all three: whether a satisfaction metric belongs in product objectives at all.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this reports the score with a trend line and a benchmark. Someone who has internalised it never reports one without four companions: the three band shares, the response rate, the confidence interval and the segment split. She asks first whether respondent composition changed, treats fewer than a thousand responses as a conversation starter, and refuses to let the score become a target.

12. What each protagonist decided

Pratyusha Vaijapurkar rewrote the slide rather than the roadmap. It showed 17.0 as 41.0 per cent promoters, 35.0 per cent passives and 24.0 per cent detractors, with an interval of ±0.40 points, split into metro at 27.0 and tier-2 at 2.0, and stated that the fall from 22.0 was mix and the March plan implied 13.25 at unchanged service. She declined the ₹3.4 crore delight programme and moved ₹1.9 crore to substitution and refund handling in tier-2 cities, setting her March goal on segment-level NPS and ninety-day repeat ordering.

Parthiv Vashishth did the opposite of celebrating. He suspended the aggregate NPS for two quarters, on the grounds that 391 responses could not support it, and replaced it with a tier-1 review: eighteen named accounts read individually, supervisor scores separated from director scores, scanner complaints routed to procurement with a named owner. He kept the reconciliation CES as the one number his team would answer for, because it pointed at a process he could change. Vasundhara Pujare argued he had discarded the only comparable series the firm had.

Discussion questions. 1. Pitara's tier-2 NPS is 2.0 against the metro core's 27.0. Service failure, harder market, or different customer — and what one datum would distinguish them? 2. Rachna's response-weighted NPS is 12.0 and its ARR-weighted NPS is 3.7. Which belongs in the board pack, and what does the answer imply about who the firm believes its customer is? 3. Rasana's incentive added fifty-three points to a score worth five points of repurchase. Would you publish the holdout figure of 2.0, and what would you put in place first?

13. Going deeper

Survey design comes next, because every metric here is one survey question whose wording and placement move the result more than product changes do; it unlocks telling a real movement from an artefact. Sampling and representativeness treats Pitara's silent majority formally. Descriptive statistics for PMs generalises section three's variance arithmetic. Conjoint and MaxDiff answers what scores cannot: what customers would trade off. Quantitative concept testing moves measurement before the build. The Sean Ellis PMF survey is the closest cousin, measuring disappointment at loss. Consumer panels and syndicated data supply the validation that rescued Rasana.

Evanta Home Services: Which Score Do We Trust?

A teaching case on NPS, CSAT and CES

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Vrinda Manchanda sat in a glass-walled meeting room on the third floor of Evanta Home Services' Indiranagar office in Bengaluru, with one slide on the screen and a deadline written on the whiteboard behind it. The board would meet on Tuesday, 27 October, twelve days before Diwali, and the founder-CEO, Vishwas Mahajan, had asked her to bring a single recommendation: which customer-satisfaction measure should Evanta publish to investors and use to pay its service professionals for the rest of the financial year?

The slide showed one number, a Net Promoter Score of +25 for the July to September quarter, down from +31 three months earlier. Vishwas wanted to put it on the board deck and to link the next quality bonus to it. Vrinda, Evanta's Chief Product Officer, had spent a decade in product teams and did not doubt that the number was real. What she doubted was how much it could carry. She had until Friday, 23 October, to send the board paper.

2. Company background

Evanta was founded in 2018 by Vishwas and two college friends who had grown tired of finding a reliable plumber through neighbours. The app now connects households in eleven cities, from Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune to Gurugram and Kochi, with about 9,400 active service professionals across three lines: deep cleaning, appliance repair and salon-at-home. In the quarter just ended, Evanta recorded revenue of ₹74.0 crore. The business sits in a market defined by Urban Company, which set the template for app-based home services in India, and by newer quick-service entrants such as Pronto, as well as the vast unorganised sector of the neighbourhood mechanic and the building's own housekeeping staff.

Evanta had always measured itself on three things without ever having decided their roles. After each completed job the app asked for a one-to-five star rating of satisfaction. Once a quarter, a sample of customers received a longer survey on the app and on WhatsApp, which repeated that satisfaction item for the customer's most recent job and also included the familiar question about how likely they were to recommend Evanta to a friend or colleague, scored from zero to ten. And in the rescheduling flow, which the app logs separately from the survey and which was introduced after a spate of Dussehra cancellations the previous year, customers who completed a reschedule were asked how much they agreed that rescheduling had been easy. Surveys were run with consent notices designed to comply with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

3. The situation

The quarterly survey went to 12,000 customers drawn at random from completed jobs, and 3,000 responded, a response rate of 25.0 per cent. Of those 3,000, 2,800 answered the recommendation question and 200 left it blank, usually after answering the satisfaction items; 2,950 answered the satisfaction item. Exhibit 1 sets the 2,800 against the 2,600 who answered the same question in the previous quarter. Promoters, who scored nine or ten, were 45.0 per cent of the 2,800 who answered, passives (seven or eight) were 35.0 per cent, and detractors (zero to six) were 20.0 per cent, giving an NPS of +25. A quarter earlier, detractors had been only 14.0 per cent of the answering base.

Vedant Mattoo, the data scientist in Toronto who built the survey pipeline, had been careful about one point from the beginning. Each percentage had to be taken over the customers who answered that particular question, not over everyone who was invited or even everyone who responded. He ran the sampling error: on 2,800 answers, the +25 carried a 95 per cent margin of about 2.8 points, so the plausible range ran from +22.2 to +27.8. The change from +31 has a 95 per cent interval of −9.9 to −2.1 points (Exhibit 1), which excludes zero, but Vedant also warned that Evanta's mix of jobs had shifted toward appliance repair between the two quarters, and he did not have the Q2 split by service line.

Exhibit 2 shows why that matters. Salon-at-home scored +47 on 600 answers; deep cleaning scored +30 on 1,000; appliance repair, the largest line at ₹38.4 crore of revenue, scored only +10 on 1,200. The headline +25 is a blend, and any change in the weights moves it without a single customer changing their mind.

Exhibit 3 gives the other two instruments. Of the 2,950 survey responders who rated their most recent job on the five-point scale (the survey item, not the all-job in-app ratings), 2,360 gave a four or five, a CSAT of 80.0 per cent. On the face of it, four in five customers were happy with the job, while promoters outnumbered detractors by only 25 points as a share of the 2,800 who answered the recommendation question. Meanwhile the app logs showed 910 customers starting to reschedule a booking in the quarter, of whom 700 completed it and 640 answered the seven-point ease question; 378 of them agreed (five to seven), or 59.1 per cent, with a mean of 4.71. Vrinda noticed that the 640 were by definition customers who had succeeded in rescheduling. The 210 who started and gave up (23.1 per cent of the 910) were never asked.

The team saw the matter from several time zones. Vamsi Mundra, Evanta's customer-success lead in Singapore, read the detractor comments every Monday and believed the appliance-repair scores were driven by quote shocks and waits for spare parts, rather than by the behaviour of technicians. Vihari Marwah, the Chief Operating Officer in Gurugram, wanted a number that technicians could move with their own conduct. A designer in Berlin, working remotely on the rescheduling flow, had already shipped two changes and asked whether the CES score would be allowed to tell her if they worked. The 6.00 am stand-up in Bengaluru was Vamsi's 8.30 am in Singapore and Vedant's 8.30 pm the previous evening in Toronto; nobody could say they had not been consulted, but few had been persuaded.

4. The people

Vishwas Mahajan, founder-CEO in Bengaluru, wants one number that investors recognise. He sees NPS as the language of the funding market and believes a bonus tied to it would focus the whole company. Vihari Marwah, Chief Operating Officer in Gurugram, runs 9,400 service professionals and wants an incentive that is fair: a technician should be paid for what the technician controls. Vamsi Mundra, customer-success lead in Singapore, wants the quarter's comments read before any score is hardwired into pay. Vedant Mattoo, data scientist in Toronto, wants each figure published with its base and its margin, and is quietly uneasy that a single dial will be asked to explain a business with three different products.

Vrinda herself wants to avoid two mistakes. The first is to treat a single-question survey as a diagnosis. The second is to answer the board's request for one number by pretending that the three instruments measure the same thing.

5. Exhibits

The three exhibits are discussed in section 3; the timeline fixes the dates against Diwali.

6. The options

Option A: Make NPS the north-star and the bonus trigger. Vishwas's preference. The company would report the +25 to the board and investors, and the quarterly quality pool of ₹1.8 crore would pay out only for service lines that reached +30 (Exhibit 2). The upside is clarity and a metric the funding community already understands. The cost is that appliance repair, at +10 and with the biggest revenue, would pay nothing, while its main drivers (quotes and spare-part waits) lie largely outside the technician's hands. Deep cleaning, at exactly +30.0 on 1,000 answers, sits on the threshold with a margin of about ±4.7 points, so its payout would turn on noise. Cutting by city instead would not help: 2,800 answers spread over eleven cities is roughly 250 each, a margin near ±9.5 points.

Option B: Pay on CSAT and publish CSAT. Vihari's preference. The in-app job rating is collected on every job (a larger base than the survey item behind Exhibit 3), so it can be computed by technician, by day and by city, and a technician can see how a visit changed it. The upside is control and speed. The cost is that a high satisfaction share says nothing about the 560 of 2,800 answering customers (20.0 per cent) who are NPS detractors; these are a different group on a different base from the 590 of 2,950 (20.0 per cent) who rated their job one to three. A rating given at the doorstep invites inflation and pressure on customers.

Option C: Assign each metric a different job and delay the incentive. Vrinda's own draft. Report NPS quarterly with its base and margin as a measure of the relationship, use CSAT as an operational signal on each job, use CES as the test of the rescheduling flow, and spend a three-month, ₹42 lakh diagnostic on appliance repair before tying any pay to NPS, while releasing a minority share of the pool, one third or ₹60 lakh, on audited job-level CSAT. The upside is that every metric answers a question it can answer. The cost is that the board asked for one number and would receive three, and the diagnostic spans the Diwali peak, when pressure to act is greatest.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. For each of the three instruments, what exactly is the population, what is the question, and what can the score not tell you? Which denominator sits under each percentage in Exhibits 1 to 3?
  2. The 200 customers who skipped the recommendation question are excluded from the +25. What would you want to know about them, and how much could they move the score?
  3. Using Exhibit 2, how much of the six-point fall in NPS could be a change in service mix rather than a change in how customers feel? What data would settle it?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 27 October, and what would you tell Vishwas about the one number he asked for?

8. A note for the learner

This case frames a common trap: treating a satisfaction score as an objective rather than as an instrument. NPS, CSAT and CES are single-question surveys with baggage. Each is cheap, each is answered by a self-selected minority, and each describes a different thing: NPS the relationship and the likelihood of advocacy, CSAT the experience of one interaction, and CES the friction in one flow. A well-reasoned answer begins with bases. The +25 is correct only over the 2,800 who answered; the 80.0 per cent is correct only over the 2,950 who answered the rating; the 59.1 per cent describes only the 640 who finished rescheduling. A good answer also separates statistical noise from structure. The change interval of −9.9 to −2.1 points (Exhibit 1) excludes zero, yet the service-line spread in Exhibit 2, from +10 to +47, is far larger than the movement being debated.

One defensible path is Option C, with a firm commitment attached. Take to the board the NPS of +25 on 2,800 answers, its margin of 2.8 points, and the three-line split, and say plainly that the quarter-on-quarter change cannot yet be attributed to customers rather than mix until the Q2 service-line cells are recovered. Keep the quality pool at ₹1.8 crore but never trigger it on NPS. Release one third, ₹60 lakh, on job-level CSAT, which technicians can influence, after auditing it for pressure on customers, and hold the remaining ₹1.2 crore until the diagnostic reports. Fund the ₹42 lakh appliance-repair work first, since that line carries ₹38.4 crore of the quarter's ₹74.0 crore. Use CES to judge the Berlin redesign, but widen its base to include the 210 customers who abandoned rescheduling, or the 59.1 per cent will flatter the flow.

Several things remain unsettled, and a good class will say so: whether the 200 non-answerers differ from the 2,800, whether CSAT or NPS better predicts rebooking, and whether investors will accept three numbers. A score tells you where to look. It does not tell you why, and it should not be asked to decide who gets paid.
exp20v2-q.nps.csat:
NPS, CSAT and CES: what a satisfaction score can and cannot tell you

Discovery and Design, Quantitative and Market Research

1. A target on a slide

On 12 October 2026, Indira Chaudhuri, head of product at Gopuram Travel Systems, a Chennai-based intercity bus ticketing platform, sat down with a one-line slide. It read: "Net Promoter Score 30 by 31 March 2027." The September survey had just closed at 15. The chief executive wanted a customer-delight programme to close the gap, and a budget of ₹120 lakh was pencilled in for loyalty perks. Hiren Gajjar, who ran customer support, wanted ₹90 lakh spent instead on fixing cancellation refunds, which took too long and generated most of his complaints.

Both men were pointing at the same number and drawing opposite conclusions. Ian Whitfield, the data scientist on Gopuram's team in Austin, had warned Indira that the number could not settle the argument by itself. If she funded the wrong option, a half-year of effort would move a score without moving a customer. If she dismissed the score, she would lose the one measure the board trusted. She needed to know what each satisfaction metric actually says, and where it falls silent.

2. The idea

A satisfaction metric is a single survey question, answered by a sample of customers, converted into one headline number. Three are in common use. The Net Promoter Score (NPS) asks, "How likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague?" on a scale of 0 to 10. Fred Reichheld of Bain & Company introduced it in a 2003 Harvard Business Review article, "The One Number You Need to Grow", as a replacement for long satisfaction questionnaires that nobody acted on. Customer Satisfaction (CSAT), the older measure, asks how satisfied the customer was with a specific experience, usually on a 1 to 5 scale. Customer Effort Score (CES) was proposed in 2010 by Matthew Dixon, Karen Freeman and Nick Toman of the Corporate Executive Board, who argued that after a service interaction, ease predicts loyalty better than delight.

The three differ in their object. NPS measures a relationship, CSAT measures an event, and CES measures friction inside an event. That is the sentence Indira could repeat in the meeting without sounding glib: "Each score is a different question about a different thing, so each can fail in a different way, and none can tell us what to fix."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics begin with a sampling frame. Gopuram sent a survey link after each completed trip in September 2026: 2,50,000 surveys. Of these, 45,000 customers responded, a response rate of 18 per cent. Every later figure here uses those 45,000, and the 2,05,000 who stayed silent are the first thing to keep in mind.

For NPS, responses are sorted into three bands. Scores of 9 and 10 are promoters, 7 and 8 are passives, and 0 to 6 are detractors. The score is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors, reported as a plain number between −100 and +100. Passives never enter the subtraction, but they remain in the denominator, so a large passive group dilutes both percentages. The implicit steps are the thresholds: the choice to call a 6 a detractor and an 8 neutral is a convention, not a discovery.

NPS = 40 − 25 = 15. The detractor count is 3,600 + 2,700 + 1,800 + 1,350 + 900 + 450 + 450 = 11,250.

CSAT is simpler. Gopuram's second question asked, "How satisfied were you with this trip?" on a 1 to 5 scale, answered by the same 45,000. The convention counts 4 and 5 as satisfied. CSAT is satisfied responses divided by total responses, and the result is a percentage, not a difference.

CES, finally, is asked only after a support contact. Gopuram's support team handled 24,000 contacts in September, and 6,000 of those customers answered "The company made it easy to handle my issue" on a 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) scale, a 25 per cent response rate. Counts for ratings 1 to 7 were 300, 420, 600, 900, 1,380, 1,500 and 900, which sum to 6,000. Ratings of 5 to 7 total 3,780, so 63 per cent agreed. Weighting each rating by its count gives 28,740, and the mean is 28,740 / 6,000 = 4.79. Both forms of CES circulate, and a team must say which it reports.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

Ian split the 45,000 by route type. Gopuram had recently added overnight sleeper routes, and these behaved differently from day seater routes.

Blended NPS is computed from the combined counts, 40% − 25%, and matches the response-weighted average: (27,000 × 7 + 18,000 × 27) / 45,000 = 675,000 / 45,000 = 15.

Now the second pass. The June 2026 wave had scored 19, and the team had read the fall to 15 as a decline in service. Ian showed otherwise. In June, sleeper customers were 40 per cent of respondents, so 0.40 × 7 + 0.60 × 27 = 2.8 + 16.2 = 19. In September, the sleeper share was 60 per cent: 0.60 × 7 + 0.40 × 27 = 4.2 + 10.8 = 15. If segment scores held steady, the whole four-point fall came from the changed mix, not from worse service. And were sleeper to reach 80 per cent of responses, the same segment scores would give 0.80 × 7 + 0.20 × 27 = 5.6 + 5.4 = 11. A company can grow the business it wants and watch its NPS fall.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Sampling error is larger than people expect

An NPS built from 45,000 responses carries a 95 per cent margin of about ±0.73 points: the variance is (0.40 + 0.25) − (0.15)² = 0.6275, so the standard error is the square root of 0.6275 / 45,000, which is 0.003734 as a proportion or about 0.37 points on the NPS scale, and 1.96 times that is 0.73 points. A single route with 400 responses and the same shares has a margin of ±7.8 points. Teams routinely celebrate movements that sit inside that band.

Non-response is not random

Only 18 per cent of those surveyed answered. Customers with a strong view, in either direction, answer more often than the indifferent middle. The score describes respondents, and the gap between respondents and the 2,05,000 silent customers is unknown.

Passives are not neutral in effect

A passive is counted as zero in the subtraction, yet 35 per cent of Gopuram's customers sit there. They are the group a competitor such as redBus can win with a coupon. A score that ignores them hides the largest pool of switchable customers.

The thresholds hide the distribution

Two businesses can both score 15 with very different shapes: one with 40 per cent promoters and 25 per cent detractors, another with 20 per cent promoters and 5 per cent detractors. Their problems and their remedies differ. Always read the three shares, never the difference alone.

NPS asks about intent, not behaviour

Recommendation is a stated intention. The evidence that it predicts growth is strongest where word of mouth drives acquisition, and weaker elsewhere. Validate the score against what customers did next: rebooking within 90 days, referrals actually redeemed.

CSAT and NPS answer different questions

A customer can be satisfied with a trip and still be unwilling to recommend a platform that is no better than the alternative. CSAT of 70 per cent beside NPS of 15 is not a contradiction. It is two instruments reading two objects.

CES locates friction but not value

CES is excellent at pointing to an expensive process. It says nothing about why a customer chose you, and a frictionless service can still be forgettable.

No score tells you what to fix

A satisfaction number is a symptom. Cause enters only through a follow-up question, free-text comments, or joins to operational data. Before relying on any score, ask who was sampled, when, with which wording, and what decision would change if the number moved.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products, early and late

In consumer products such as Gopuram's, volumes are high and relationships thin, so transactional CSAT and CES run continuously and NPS is tracked in quarterly waves. In B2B, a company may have only 80 customers, so an NPS figure is a handful of names. The sensible practice there is to read each response by account, weight by contract value, and follow up personally; the buyer and the daily user often disagree, and averaging them conceals it. A marketplace has two sides. Gopuram's bus operators are customers too, and a rider NPS of 15 says nothing about whether operators will stay. Each side needs its own survey, and a gain for one can cost the other. Early-stage firms cannot reach a stable score; with 200 responses the margin is about ±11 points, so conversations beat dashboards. Large firms can measure precisely, and their danger changes: the score becomes a target, and a number that is managed stops measuring.

7. Common mistakes

Tying incentives to the score

Symptom: conductors and agents ask riders for a "10". The misunderstanding is that the score is the goal. The cheapest diagnostic is to compare the share of 10s against the share of 9s: a sudden cliff-edge at 10, with few 9s, signals coaching.

Comparing waves without checking mix

Symptom: a four-point fall triggers a service review. The misunderstanding is that a blended score moves only when quality moves. Recompute last quarter's score using this quarter's segment weights before concluding anything.

Reporting a mean as if it were NPS or CSAT

Symptom: a dashboard says "CES 4.8" in one slide and "63 per cent" in another. The misunderstanding is that the scale defines the metric. Write the formula beside every number.

Treating the score as a diagnosis

Symptom: a team debates "why is NPS low?" without any comments to read. The cheapest diagnostic is reading fifty verbatim detractor comments before any meeting.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Indira's slide would have read differently. It would show 15 as 40 per cent promoters, 25 per cent detractors and 35 per cent passives, with a margin of ±0.73 points, split by sleeper (7) and day seater (27), and beside it a CSAT of 70 per cent and a refund-flow CES of 63 per cent agreeing. It would state that the June-to-September fall was mix, name the response rate of 18 per cent, and attach a hundred coded detractor comments. The goal would be set on behaviour the score is meant to predict, with the score as a guardrail.

9. What Indira decided

Indira read fifty detractor comments with Hiren and found that refund delay appeared in more than a third of them; it also dominated the low end of the CES responses, where 1,320 customers rated 1 to 3 against 3,780 who agreed. She declined the March target of 30 and proposed instead: cut median refund time, track CES on the refund flow, and report NPS by segment with its margin. She backed the ₹90 lakh refund fix, and held the ₹120 lakh perks programme for a test on a single route, so that the claim "delight raises recommendation" would have evidence before it had a budget. Her reasoning was that a score cannot say what to build, but the comments and the effort data could.

To go further, study survey design, since every metric here is a survey question with its own wording and sampling baggage, and then cohort and retention analysis, which tests whether any score predicts what customers do.

Two questions to sit with. If Gopuram's response rate were 5 per cent rather than 18, which conclusions in this case would you withdraw first? And what would you need to see before agreeing that a number of 30 meant customers were better off, not merely better managed?
